answer_text:
Interpreting \(f^{(1989)}\) as the \(1989\)-th derivative, the answer is yes.

Let

\[
g(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}.
\]

The function \(g\) is continuous on \(\mathbf{R}^{+}=(0,\infty)\). We can repeatedly integrate it. Define functions recursively by

\[
F_0(x)=g(x),
\]

and for \(k=1,2,\dots,1989\),

\[
F_k(x)=\int_{1}^{x} F_{k-1}(t)\,dt.
\]

Since \(F_{k-1}\) is continuous, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives

\[
F_k'(x)=F_{k-1}(x).
\]

Thus by induction,

\[
F_k^{(k)}(x)=F_0(x)=g(x)
\]

for every \(k\le 1989\). In particular, setting

\[
f(x)=F_{1989}(x)
\]

gives a real-valued function on \((0,\infty)\) such that

\[
f^{(1989)}(x)=g(x)=\frac{x}{x+1}.
\]

Equivalently, one explicit particular solution is

\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{1988!}\int_{1}^{x} (x-t)^{1988}\frac{t}{t+1}\,dt.
\]

Therefore such a mapping exists.

\[
\boxed{\text{Yes}}
\]
